newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Mercenary deal should not affect poll -PNG's Chan.
newsitem.headline: Mercenary deal should not affect poll -PNG's Chan.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius said on Friday on the eve of national elections that voters should not be swayed by a mercenary crisis which almost toppled his government two months ago.

Up to three million citizens will begin voting on Saturday in the South Pacific nation's most important election since independence and the poll is likely to be dominated by concerns over Chan's failure to put down a secessionist rebellion.

Chan stepped aside in March while a commission of inquiry examined a US$36 million deal to hire African mercenaries through London-based military consultancy Sandline International to quash the nine-year rebellion on nearby Bougainville island.
Chan returned to office last week at the end of his current four-year term saying the inquiry had cleared him and two senior ministers of any wrongdoing.
"Do not let the Sandline crisis cloud your thinking," Chan said in a statement issued by his People's Progress Party.
"Do not judge what Papua New Guinea has experienced only on the Bougainville crisis."
The election will see all four men who have served as prime minister since independence from Australia in 1975 challenge for the post again.
Sir Michael Somare and Paias Wingti have both served as premier twice before and Sir Rabbie Namaliu once.

Somare, the country's first post-independence prime minister, said during campaigning on Friday that the two days of civil unrest sparked by the mercenary deal showed how the country could make its leaders accountable for their actions.
"The Sandline crisis was a real victory to ordinary, concerned Papua New Guineans," Somare said.
"The people of Papua New Guinea wanted an end to the whispers of corruption in high places."
Party politics have little relevance in Papua New Guinea and the prime minister will be chosen by a vote from the floor of the 109-seat parliament.
A record 2,368 candidates -- 1,665 of them independents -- have nominated across the country's 19 regions.

Voting will last for two weeks to allow voters from the remote Highlands region to travel to polling stations. Another week has been set aside for counting and the the new government will be formed after parliament is sworn in on July 15.
More than 1,000 police and 450 soldiers have been flown to the Highlands to prevent repeats of the violence which has marked past previous elections.
A nationwide liquor ban and dusk-to-dawn night curfew have also been imposed.
